extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, and newsroom leaders covering sensitive or traumatic stories
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for journalists and news organizations on ethical choices when reporting, packaging, and promoting stories that involve victims, tragedy, or graphic material, with attention to minimizing harm and respecting privacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat subjects as human beings deserving of respect
rubrics_metrics.description: “Ethical journalists treat sources [and] subjects as human beings deserving of respect.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dehumanize or exploit people who appear in reporting; consider how coverage affects their dignity and wellbeing. Avoid describing subjects in ways that reduce them to objects of curiosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid highlighting incidents out of context
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should not...highlight incidents out of context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide contextualization rather than sensational snippets that distort events or imply false narratives about subjects; avoid using isolated details to drive traffic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sensitive when seeking or using interviews/photographs of those affected by tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: “Be sensitive when seeking or using interviews or photographs of those affected by tragedy or grief. Show compassion for those who may be affected adversely by news coverage. Avoid pandering to lurid curiosity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise restraint when asking for or publishing images/quotes from grieving people; prioritize consent, minimize intrusion, and avoid gratuitous depictions of suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat people appearing in content with fairness and respect (producer standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Producers should treat the people who are the subjects of, who appear in, or who are referenced in the content they produce with fairness and respect.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply fairness in selection, editing, and presentation; avoid manipulative editing or placement that misrepresents individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid insensitivity to tragedy or grief (unprofessional conduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of unprofessional conduct by a producer include…insensitivity to tragedy or grief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag gestures, language, or editorial choices that trivialize or sensationalize victims’ suffering as violations of professional standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: When material is controversial or sensitive, let good taste prevail
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases that present a dilemma about whether to include 'controversial or sensitive material' such as 'extreme violence…or [content] that is morbid, sensational, or gratuitously offensive to general taste' the guidelines insist that 'good taste must prevail.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use editorial judgment to exclude graphic or sensational content unless it is essential and handled with care; prefer restraint over shock value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Just because material is public record doesn't make amplification appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: “Just because something is legally public does not make it right for journalists to amplify it across as many platforms as possible.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider privacy norms and the original purpose of records held in relative obscurity; avoid wide distribution of sensitive public records unless clearly necessary to the public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit use of publicly available material in promotional/online content
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple solutions could include guidelines or limits in how publicly available information is used in promotional and online material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create explicit rules about what archival/court material may be used in teasers, social posts, and promos to avoid re-victimization and gratuitous exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using intimate/traumatic audio/video as promotional bait
rubrics_metrics.description: Promotional teasers on social media featuring frantic 9-1-1 audio or visible images of a deceased person can re-victimize families.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use raw 9-1-1 calls, graphic footage, or plaintive audio as click-driving previews; promotional content should be vetted for potential harm and dignity impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish 9-1-1 calls only when critical to the story; avoid as promos
rubrics_metrics.description: There are times when publishing a 9-1-1 call is critical to a story, but if journalists continually use 9-1-1 calls as promotional material and then post on Twitter, will people think twice before calling emergency services?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess public-interest value vs. public-safety and privacy consequences before publishing or promoting emergency call recordings; avoid routine promotional use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep ethics front-and-center with checklists for deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Media organizations could provide a checklist for everyone working on a story to keep their code of ethics front and center as deadlines get met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement practical tools (checklists, sign-offs) during production and promotion workflows to ensure ethical considerations are not overridden by time pressure or traffic incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a 'do-less-harm' policy and embrace empathy
rubrics_metrics.description: “Perhaps it’s time to embrace a do-less-harm policy, one that embraces a more generous dose of empathy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutionalize norms prioritizing harm reduction (e.g., extra review for trauma-sensitive elements, consultation with affected parties) and center empathy in editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit or reconsider immersive recreations (e.g., VR) for traumatic scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Plans for a virtual reality experience of the crime scene raised concerns about putting such content online; the claim that VR would reach fewer people was questioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate reach and re-traumatization risk of immersive formats; do not assume limited distribution—assess ethical implications before producing immersive reconstructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include only material essential to telling the story; avoid sensational details
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors stated they 'took great pains to avoid sensational details and to include only material essential to telling this important story.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trim graphic or extraneous details unless they are indispensable to accuracy or public understanding; prioritize necessity over salaciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh newsworthiness against family grief and privacy harms
rubrics_metrics.description: Question whether editorial teams put their own commercial and professional interests ahead of a family’s grief; balance the story’s newsworthiness with its impact on victims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit trade-off assessments: who benefits from publication, what harm may result, and whether less harmful alternatives exist (anonymization, summaries, content warnings).
